items.title: The fixed-endpoint second variation of a time-dependent action at a curve
items.reference: batch-12-local-construction; the fixed-endpoint family of D. Cline, Variational Principles, Sections 5.1-5.2, materialised as a definition and recorded in the batch notes
items.statement:
Let $n\ge1$, let $a<b$ be reals, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and nonempty, and let
$(O,\mathcal L)$ be a time-dependent Lagrangian chart over $[a,b]\times U$ in the sense of
[[def-cm-time-dependent-lagrangian-and-action]]: $O\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n$
is open with

$$[a,b]\times U\times\mathbb R^n\subseteq O,$$

and $\mathcal L:O\to\mathbb R$ is of class $C^2$. Recall from that definition that a $C^2$ curve
$q:[a,b]\to U$ is the restriction to $[a,b]$ of a $C^2$ map on an open interval, that a
**variation** of $q$ is such a map $\eta:[a,b]\to\mathbb R^n$ with

$$\eta(a)=\eta(b)=0,$$

and that the **action** of a $C^2$ curve is

$$S(q):=\int_a^b\mathcal L\bigl(t,q(t),q'(t)\bigr)\,dt .$$

**The fixed-endpoint family.** Let $q:[a,b]\to U$ be a $C^2$ curve and let $\eta$ be a variation
of $q$. For $\varepsilon\in\mathbb R$ put

$$q_\varepsilon(t):=q(t)+\varepsilon\eta(t)\qquad(t\in[a,b]).$$

By clause 1 of [[lem-cm-first-variation-formula]] there is $\varepsilon_0>0$ such that
$q_\varepsilon$ is a $C^2$ admissible curve with values in $U$ for every
$\varepsilon\in(-\varepsilon_0,\varepsilon_0)$, so that the action $S(q_\varepsilon)$ is defined
for those $\varepsilon$.

**The second variation.** The **second variation of $S$ at $q$ in the direction $\eta$** is the
second derivative at $\varepsilon=0$ of the function $\varepsilon\mapsto S(q+\varepsilon\eta)$:

$$\delta^2S(q)[\eta,\eta]:=\frac{d^2}{d\varepsilon^2}\Big|_{\varepsilon=0}S(q+\varepsilon\eta).$$

This is a well-defined real number under the present hypotheses: the map
$\varepsilon\mapsto S(q+\varepsilon\eta)$ is twice differentiable at $0$, with the explicit
integral formula, by [[lem-cm-second-variation-formula]], which depends on this definition only
for the notation $\delta^2S(q)[\eta,\eta]$. The value is a single real number determined by the
pair $(q,\eta)$ and does not depend on the choice of the $C^2$ extensions of $q$ and $\eta$, since
the values of $q_\varepsilon$ and $q_\varepsilon'$ on $[a,b]$ are those of any such extension and
the derivative on $[a,b]$ is extension-independent
([[def-cm-time-dependent-lagrangian-and-action]]).

**Scope.** The definition introduces the one-parameter family and its second derivative at
$\varepsilon=0$, nothing else. It asserts nothing about minimising or maximising $S$, nothing
about the sign of $\delta^2S$, and no physical interpretation of $\mathcal L$; stationarity of a
curve is the separate first-order condition recorded in
[[def-cm-time-dependent-lagrangian-and-action]], and no equivalence with the vanishing of an
Euler-Lagrange expression is used at this point.
items.strategy: Define the family and the second derivative with the chart and extension conventions of def-cm-time-dependent-lagrangian-and-action; state the well-definedness and its exact source without proving it here.

items.title: The second variation of a time-dependent action: twice differentiability of the fixed-endpoint family and the Hessian integral formula
items.reference: expansion-proofs.md#e19 (the second-order step that the prose section differentiates silently)
items.statement:
Let $(O,\mathcal L)$ be a time-dependent Lagrangian chart over $[a,b]\times U$ in the sense of
[[def-cm-time-dependent-lagrangian-and-action]] (so $\mathcal L$ is $C^2$ and
$[a,b]\times U\times\mathbb R^n\subseteq O$), let $q:[a,b]\to U$ be a $C^2$ curve and let $\eta$
be a variation of $q$ (a $C^2$ map with $\eta(a)=\eta(b)=0$). Write
$\psi(\varepsilon,t):=\bigl(t,q(t)+\varepsilon\eta(t),q'(t)+\varepsilon\eta'(t)\bigr)$ and, for
$|\varepsilon|<\varepsilon_0$ with $\varepsilon_0$ as in clause 1 below,

$$H(\varepsilon,t):=\sum_{j,k=1}^n\Bigl[\frac{\partial^2\mathcal L}{\partial q_j\partial q_k}\bigl(\psi(\varepsilon,t)\bigr)\eta_j(t)\eta_k(t)+2\frac{\partial^2\mathcal L}{\partial q_j\partial v_k}\bigl(\psi(\varepsilon,t)\bigr)\eta_j(t)\eta_k'(t)+\frac{\partial^2\mathcal L}{\partial v_j\partial v_k}\bigl(\psi(\varepsilon,t)\bigr)\eta_j'(t)\eta_k'(t)\Bigr].$$

Then:

1. there is $\varepsilon_0>0$ such that for every $\varepsilon\in(-\varepsilon_0,\varepsilon_0)$
   the curve $q+\varepsilon\eta$ is a $C^2$ admissible curve with values in $U$, and the map
   $\varepsilon\mapsto S(q+\varepsilon\eta)$ is of class $C^2$ on $(-\varepsilon_0,\varepsilon_0)$;
2. for every $\varepsilon\in(-\varepsilon_0,\varepsilon_0)$,

$$\frac{d^2}{d\varepsilon^2}S(q+\varepsilon\eta)=\int_a^bH(\varepsilon,t)\,dt ;$$

3. in particular the second variation of [[def-cm-second-variation-of-the-action]] is

$$\delta^2S(q)[\eta,\eta]=\int_a^bH(0,t)\,dt,$$

the formula of clause 2 with every second partial of $\mathcal L$ evaluated at
$\bigl(t,q(t),q'(t)\bigr)$.
items.strategy: Apply the compact-rectangle differentiation theorem twice: the first epsilon-derivative is the first-variation integrand, the second is the chain-rule derivative of that integrand along the affine family, computed with the C^1 gradients L_q and L_v; symmetrise the mixed sums by Clairaut.

references.title: D. Cline, Variational Principles in Classical Mechanics (2nd edition, University of Rochester River Campus Libraries, open textbook, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), Sections 5.1-5.2: the parametric family and the first-variation computation; the second variation is not treated there
D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (University of Cambridge Part II Mathematical Tripos), Section 2.1: the first variation of the action with fixed endpoints, printed pages 11-12

items.title: Second variation of the oscillator action on a finite interval: both signs for $T>\pi/\omega$ and the value at $T=\pi/\omega$
items.statement:
Let $\omega>0$ and $T>0$, let $U:=\mathbb R$, and consider the time-dependent Lagrangian chart
over $[0,T]\times U$ with $O:=\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R$ and
$\mathcal L(q,v):=\tfrac12\bigl(v^2-\omega^2q^2\bigr)$
([[def-cm-time-dependent-lagrangian-and-action]]). Write $S$ for its action and $\delta^2S$ for
the second variation of [[def-cm-second-variation-of-the-action]]. Then:

1. the zero curve $q_0\equiv0$ is a $C^2$ admissible curve and is stationary for $S$;
2. for every integer $n\ge1$ the map $\eta_n(t):=\sin(n\pi t/T)$ is a variation of $q_0$, and

$$\delta^2S(q_0)[\eta_n,\eta_n]=\frac T2\Bigl(\Bigl(\frac{n\pi}{T}\Bigr)^2-\omega^2\Bigr);$$

moreover $S(\varepsilon\eta_n)=\frac{\varepsilon^2}{2}\delta^2S(q_0)[\eta_n,\eta_n]$ for every
real $\varepsilon$;
3. if $T>\pi/\omega$, then $\delta^2S(q_0)[\eta_1,\eta_1]<0$ and
$\delta^2S(q_0)[\eta_n,\eta_n]>0$ for every integer $n>\omega T/\pi$. Consequently, for every real
$\delta_0>0$ there exist variations $\eta$ of $q_0$ with
$\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\bigl(|\eta(t)|+|\eta'(t)|+|\eta''(t)|\bigr)<\delta_0$ and $S(\eta)<0$, and
variations with the same bound and $S(\eta)>0$; hence the zero curve is neither a local minimiser
nor a local maximiser of $S$, in the sense that every neighbourhood of $q_0$ for the supremum
distance $\sup_{[0,T]}(|q-q_0|+|q'-q_0'|+|q''-q_0''|)$ contains curves whose action is below
$S(q_0)$ and curves whose action is above $S(q_0)$;
4. if $T=\pi/\omega$, then $\delta^2S(q_0)[\eta_1,\eta_1]=0$, while
$\delta^2S(q_0)[\eta_n,\eta_n]>0$ for every integer $n\ge2$.
items.strategy: Compute the second variation with the Hessian formula, evaluate the elementary trigonometric integrals by the fundamental theorem of calculus, obtain the exact action along the family from the degree-two homogeneity of L, and read off the signs using the Archimedean property to select a large n.

items.title: The undamped oscillator: Dirichlet non-uniqueness at $T=n\pi/\omega$ despite unique initial-value solutions
items.statement:
Let $m>0$ and $k>0$, put $\omega:=(k/m)^{1/2}>0$ ([[thm-of-square-roots]]), and let $T>0$.
Consider the undamped homogeneous oscillator equation

$$m\,x''(t)+k\,x(t)=0$$

of [[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]] with time domain $I=\mathbb R$ and zero forcing, and its solutions on intervals with nonempty interior. The Dirichlet curves below are restrictions to $[0,T]$ of its global solutions. Then:

1. for every real $A$ the function $x_A(t):=A\sin(\omega t)$ is a $C^2$ (indeed $C^\infty$)
   solution on $\mathbb R$ with $x_A(0)=0$ and $x_A(T)=A\sin(\omega T)$; moreover $x_A(T)=0$ if
   and only if $A=0$ or $\omega T\in\pi\mathbb Z$
   ([[thm-sine-cosine-zero-sets-and-fundamental-period]]);
2. if $T=n\pi/\omega$ for some integer $n\ge1$, then the set of $C^2$ solutions of the Dirichlet
   problem on $[0,T]$,

$$m\,x''+k\,x=0,\qquad x(0)=x(T)=0,$$

   is exactly $\{x_A:A\in\mathbb R\}$; this set is a one-dimensional real vector space, so the
   boundary-value problem has infinitely many distinct solutions with the same endpoint data
   $(0,0)$, one for each initial velocity $A\omega$;
3. by contrast, for every $(x_0,v_0)\in\mathbb R^2$ the initial-value problem
   $m\,x''+k\,x=0$, $x(0)=x_0$, $x'(0)=v_0$, has exactly one solution on $\mathbb R$, namely
   $x(t)=x_0\cos(\omega t)+(v_0/\omega)\sin(\omega t)$
   ([[thm-cm-homogeneous-oscillator-solution-classification]], clauses 3 and 4 with $c=0$);
   uniqueness for the initial-value problem therefore does not imply uniqueness for the
   boundary-value problem;
4. for the chart with $O=\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R$ and
   $\mathcal L(q,v)=\tfrac12(v^2-\omega^2q^2)$ over $[0,T]\times\mathbb R$
   ([[def-cm-time-dependent-lagrangian-and-action]]), each $x_A$ is a stationary curve of the
   action; and if $T=n\pi/\omega$, the stationary curves on $[0,T]$ satisfying the endpoint
   conditions $x(0)=x(T)=0$ are exactly the curves $x_A$, so the fixed-endpoint problem with zero
   data has infinitely many stationary curves ([[thm-cm-stationarity-iff-euler-lagrange]]).
items.strategy: Verify the explicit family by differentiation, determine its endpoint values from the zero set of the sine, classify all Dirichlet solutions through the oscillator solution classification theorem, and identify stationarity with the Euler-Lagrange expression.

references.title: K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics: Classical Mechanics (complete volume), Chapter 5 Section 5.1, Eqs. (5.1)-(5.3): the harmonic oscillator equation and its two-constant oscillatory solution, printed pages 1-2 of Chapter 5 (PDF pages 87-88)

D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (University of Cambridge Part II Mathematical Tripos), Section 2.6 and the start of Section 2.6.1, printed pages 37-41: linearised oscillations about an equilibrium with arbitrary two-constant families, and the statement that the solution of a linearised system matches prescribed initial data uniquely

items.title: The inertia tensor of a finite bounded Borel measure about any point of $\mathbb R^3$
items.reference: expansion-proofs.md#e19 (the shifted integrand of the parallel-axis computation, materialised as a definition and recorded in the batch notes)
items.statement:
Let $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^3)$ be the Borel sigma-algebra of $\mathbb R^3$
([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]), let $\nu$ be a measure on the measurable space
$(\mathbb R^3,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^3))$ ([[def-measure]], [[def-measure-space]]) that is
**finite** and **bounded**: $\nu(\mathbb R^3)<+\infty$ and
$\nu\bigl(\mathbb R^3\setminus\overline B_R(0)\bigr)=0$ for some real $R>0$
([[def-metric-ball]]). Put $m:=\nu(\mathbb R^3)\in[0,+\infty)$; nonnegativity follows from the
definition of measure [[def-measure]]. If $m>0$, then $\nu$ is a mass distribution in the sense of
[[def-cm-mass-distribution-and-inertia-matrix]]. If $m=0$, then for every Borel set
$E\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ one has $0\le\nu(E)\le\nu(\mathbb R^3)=0$, so $\nu$ is the zero measure.
Integrals against $\nu$ are Lebesgue integrals as in [[def-integral-over-a-measurable-set]] and
[[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], defined componentwise for
vector- and matrix-valued integrands. When $m>0$, recall that the inertia matrix of $\nu$ is

$$I(\nu)=\int\bigl(\lVert\rho\rVert_2^2I_3-\rho\rho^{\mathsf T}\bigr)\,d\nu(\rho)\in M_3(\mathbb R),$$

with $I_3$ the identity matrix and entrywise integrals
$I(\nu)_{jk}=\int(\lVert\rho\rVert_2^2\delta_{jk}-\rho_j\rho_k)\,d\nu$, where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$
and the matrix conventions are those of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]],
[[def-matrix-space]] and [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]].

**Shifted integrand and inertia tensor about a point.** For $a\in\mathbb R^3$ define the
component functions

$$G_a(\rho)_{jk}:=\lVert\rho-a\rVert_2^2\,\delta_{jk}-(\rho_j-a_j)(\rho_k-a_k)\qquad(j,k\in\{1,2,3\}),$$

equivalently the matrix-valued function
$G_a(\rho)=\lVert\rho-a\rVert_2^2I_3-(\rho-a)(\rho-a)^{\mathsf T}$, and define the **inertia
tensor of $\nu$ about $a$** $I_\nu(a)\in M_3(\mathbb R)$ by its entries

$$I_\nu(a)_{jk}:=\int G_a(\rho)_{jk}\,d\nu(\rho).$$

Under the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) each entry is
a finite real number; this is the content of [[lem-cm-inertia-tensor-about-a-point-is-finite]],
which depends on this definition only for its notation. For $a=0$ the shifted integrand is the
parent integrand $\lVert\rho\rVert_2^2I_3-\rho\rho^{\mathsf T}$. Thus
$I_\nu(0)=I(\nu)$ when $m>0$; if $m=0$, the parent definition does not define $I(\nu)$, while
the shifted integral remains defined and equals the zero matrix $0_{3\times3}$ for every $a$.

**Scope.** The definition names a mathematical function $a\mapsto I_\nu(a)$ from $\mathbb R^3$ to
$M_3(\mathbb R)$ determined by any finite bounded Borel measure $\nu$ and its coordinate origin.
For the zero measure this function is identically $0_{3\times3}$. No physical body, unit system or
measured mass is asserted. No translation identity for nonzero $a$ is asserted here; the centred,
positive-total-mass case is proved separately on this page.
items.strategy: Define the shifted integrand and its componentwise integral against the measure with the conventions of def-cm-mass-distribution-and-inertia-matrix; declare the finiteness result that makes the entries well-defined.

items.title: Finiteness and a uniform bound for the entries of the inertia tensor about an arbitrary point
items.reference: batch-12-local-construction; the finiteness/boundedness step added to make the shifted inertia tensor well-defined, recorded in the batch notes
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\nu$ be
a measure on $(\mathbb R^3,\mathcal B(\mathbb R^3))$ that is finite and bounded:
$\nu(\mathbb R^3)<+\infty$ and $\nu\bigl(\mathbb R^3\setminus\overline B_R(0)\bigr)=0$ for some
real $R>0$ ([[def-metric-ball]]), and let $a\in\mathbb R^3$. With the shifted integrands
$G_a(\rho)_{jk}=\lVert\rho-a\rVert_2^2\delta_{jk}-(\rho_j-a_j)(\rho_k-a_k)$ of
[[def-cm-inertia-tensor-about-a-point]] ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]] for the norm), then:

1. for all $j,k$ the function $G_a(\cdot)_{jk}:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ is Borel measurable and
   $\nu$-integrable
   ([[def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn]]);
2. each entry $I_\nu(a)_{jk}$ is a finite real number and

$$\bigl|I_\nu(a)_{jk}\bigr|\le 2\bigl(R+\lVert a\rVert_2\bigr)^2\,\nu(\mathbb R^3).$$
items.strategy: Prove measurability of the continuous polynomial integrands, bound the integrand on the support ball by the constant 2(R+||a||)^2 using the triangle inequality and the elementary inequality 2uv<=u^2+v^2, and integrate the constant against the finite measure.

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, 2015), §3.2.1, Eqs. (3.25)-(3.26), printed pp. 52-53: the shifted-integrand expansion whose boundedness makes the displaced inertia tensor finite for a bounded body

K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics: Classical Mechanics, Chapter 4 Section 4.2, Eqs. (4.27)-(4.28), printed page 6 of Chapter 4 (PDF page 60): the shifted inertia integral is a finite combination of second moments of a bounded body

items.title: Parallel-axis theorem: the inertia tensor about a displaced point of a centred mass distribution
items.statement:
Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), used only
to make the displayed integrals finite. Let $\nu$ be a mass distribution on $\mathbb R^3$ with
total mass $m=\nu(\mathbb R^3)\in(0,+\infty)$ that is **centred**, that is,
$\mu(\nu)=\int\rho\,d\nu(\rho)=0\in\mathbb R^3$
([[def-cm-mass-distribution-and-inertia-matrix]]), and let $I(\nu)$ be its inertia matrix. Then
for every $a\in\mathbb R^3$ the inertia tensor of $\nu$ about $a$
([[def-cm-inertia-tensor-about-a-point]]) satisfies

$$I_\nu(a)=I(\nu)+m\bigl(\lVert a\rVert_2^2I_3-aa^{\mathsf T}\bigr),$$

where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is the Euclidean norm, $I_3$ the identity matrix and
$aa^{\mathsf T}$ the matrix product of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]],
[[def-matrix-space]] and [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]. Entrywise,

$$I_\nu(a)_{jk}=I(\nu)_{jk}+m\bigl(\lVert a\rVert_2^2\delta_{jk}-a_ja_k\bigr)\qquad(j,k\in\{1,2,3\}).$$
items.strategy: Expand ||rho-a||^2 and (rho-a)(rho-a)^T, integrate the finite real combination termwise by L^1 linearity, and cancel the first-moment terms by the centredness hypothesis.

references.title: D. Tong, Classical Dynamics (Cambridge lecture notes, 2015), §3.2.1, Eqs. (3.25)-(3.26), printed pp. 52-53: claim and proof that (I_c)_{ab}=(I_{c.o.m})_{ab}+M(c^2delta_{ab}-c_ac_b) when the linear terms vanish in the centre-of-mass frame

K. Likharev, Essential Graduate Physics: Classical Mechanics, Chapter 4 Section 4.2, Eqs. (4.27)-(4.29), printed pages 6-7 of Chapter 4 (PDF pages 60-61): the axis-shift theorem obtained by expanding the shifted inertia integral and using that the first moments vanish in the centre-of-mass frame

items.title: Two equal masses with two outer springs and a coupling spring: eigenmodes, decoupling and the explicit normal frequencies
items.statement:
Let $m>0$, $k\ge0$ and $c\ge0$, and put

$$K:=\begin{pmatrix}k+c&-c\\-c&k+c\end{pmatrix},\qquad u_+:=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix},\qquad u_-:=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix},$$

and $\omega_+:=(k/m)^{1/2}$, $\omega_-:=((k+2c)/m)^{1/2}$ (nonnegative square roots,
[[thm-of-square-roots]]). Consider the linear system

$$m\,x''(t)=-Kx(t)$$

for $C^2$ curves $x:J\to\mathbb R^2$ on intervals $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ with nonempty interior
([[def-interval]], [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). The vector equation and its scalar mode equations are autonomous equations with time domain $\mathbb R$; a solution on $J$ is their restriction to that solution interval. Every such local solution extends uniquely to the displayed global family. Global growth claims below refer to that extension. Then:

1. $Ku_+=ku_+$ and $Ku_-=(k+2c)u_-$; the vectors $u_+,u_-$ are orthonormal, and every
   $x\in\mathbb R^2$ satisfies $x=\langle u_+,x\rangle u_++\langle u_-,x\rangle u_-$
   ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]);
2. $x$ is a solution if and only if there are solutions $y_+,y_-:J\to\mathbb R$ of the scalar
   equations

$$m\,y_+''+k\,y_+=0,\qquad m\,y_-''+(k+2c)\,y_-=0$$

   of [[def-cm-oscillator-model-and-phase-system]] with $x=y_+u_++y_-u_-$; the pair
   $(y_+,y_-)$ is unique and is given by $y_\pm=\langle u_\pm,x\rangle$;
3. consequently, for $k>0$ the solutions are exactly the curves

$$x(t)=\bigl(A_+\cos(\omega_+t)+B_+\sin(\omega_+t)\bigr)u_++\bigl(A_-\cos(\omega_-t)+B_-\sin(\omega_-t)\bigr)u_-\qquad(A_\pm,B_\pm\in\mathbb R),$$

   that is, the system is a superposition of an in-phase normal mode with squared frequency
   $k/m$ and an anti-phase normal mode with squared frequency $(k+2c)/m$
   ([[thm-cm-homogeneous-oscillator-solution-classification]]);
4. if $k=0$ and $c\ge0$, then $Ku_+=0$, and the curves $x(t)=(A+Bt)u_+$
   ($A,B\in\mathbb R$) are solutions; for $B\ne0$ each such curve has a global extension unbounded on $[0,\infty)$, so
   the zero-frequency mode is affine rather than oscillatory. The bijection of clause 2 remains
   valid with the scalar equations $m\,y_+''=0$ and $m\,y_-''+2c\,y_-=0$, and for $c>0$ the
   $u_-$-component is the trigonometric family with $\omega_-=(2c/m)^{1/2}$
   ([[thm-cm-homogeneous-oscillator-solution-classification]]); if $c=0$, it is affine as well
   ([[prop-cm-oscillator-degenerate-and-repulsive-cases]]).
items.strategy: Verify the eigenrelations and orthonormality by matrix multiplication, prove the decoupling bijection by pulling the system back along the eigenbasis and conversely reassembling two scalar solutions, and read the scalar solution families off the oscillator classification theorem.

D. items.title: The pendulum field near the downward equilibrium: bounded force derivative, cubic remainder and the finite-time small-angle error bound
items.reference: expansion-proofs.md#e19 (the E8 instantiation θ''=-(g/l) sin θ with cubic remainder)
items.statement:
Let $g>0$ and $l>0$, put $\omega:=(g/l)^{1/2}>0$ ([[thm-of-square-roots]]), and define the field

$$F:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R^2,\qquad F(\theta,v):=\bigl(v,-\omega^2\sin\theta\bigr),$$

so that $z'=F(z)$ for $z=(\theta,v)$ is the first-order form of the pendulum equation
$\theta''=-\omega^2\sin\theta$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]] for the
componentwise first-order reduction). Put

$$A:=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-\omega^2&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad L:=\max\{1,\omega^2\}.$$

Then:

1. $F$ is of class $C^\infty$ (in particular continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state
   variable), $F(0)=0$, $A=DF(0)$ is the total derivative of $F$ at the origin, and for every
   $r>0$ and every $z=(\theta,v)$ with $\lVert z\rVert_2\le r$ ([[def-metric-ball]] for the ball,
   [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] for the norm)

$$\lVert F(z)-Az\rVert_2=\omega^2\lvert\sin\theta-\theta\rvert\le\frac{\omega^2}{6}\lvert\theta\rvert^3\le\frac{\omega^2r}{6}\lVert z\rVert_2^2,\qquad\lVert F(z)\rVert_2\le L\lVert z\rVert_2 ;$$

   moreover $F$ is globally Lipschitz in the state variable with constant $L$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]), and the operator norm of $A$ for the Euclidean norm is
   $\lVert A\rVert=L$ ([[def-operator-norm]]);
2. let $z_0\in\mathbb R^2$ with $\delta:=\lVert z_0\rVert_2>0$, let $T>0$ and $r>0$ satisfy
   $\delta e^{LT}<r$, and let $y:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^2$ be the solution of the linear initial
   value problem $y'=Ay$, $y(0)=z_0$
   ([[cor-cm-variation-of-constants-for-linear-systems]]). Then the maximal solution $z$ of
   $z'=F(z)$, $z(0)=z_0$, is defined on $[0,T]$ with $\lVert z(t)\rVert_2\le\delta e^{Lt}$ for
   $t\in[0,T]$, and for every $t\in[0,T]$

$$\lVert z(t)-y(t)\rVert_2\le\frac{\omega^2r}{6}\delta^2\int_0^te^{\lVert A\rVert(t-s)}e^{2Ls}\,ds\le\frac{\omega^2r}{6}\delta^2\,t\,e^{(\lVert A\rVert+2L)t}$$

   ([[thm-cm-finite-time-linearization-error-bound]]);
3. the linear system $y'=Ay$ is the linearised pendulum: writing $y=(y_1,y_2)$ one has
   $y_1''=-\omega^2y_1$ and $y_2=y_1'$, and the first components satisfy
   $\lvert z_1(t)-y_1(t)\rvert\le\lVert z(t)-y(t)\rVert_2$ with the bounds of clause 2. The
   estimate is a finite-time statement of order $\delta^2$: it neither states nor implies that the
   nonlinear pendulum is exactly harmonic, and it makes no claim beyond $[0,T]$.
items.strategy: Compute the total derivative of F, bound the quadratic remainder by the cubic Taylor estimate for the sine, identify the Lipschitz and operator norms, and instantiate thm-cm-finite-time-linearization-error-bound.

items.title: An explicit saddle of the oscillator action at $T=2\pi$: the two variations $\sin(t/2)$ and $\sin(3t/2)$
items.reference: batch-12-constructed-B-example; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement:
Fix $\omega=1$ and $T=2\pi$ in the chart $\mathcal L(q,v)=\tfrac12(v^2-q^2)$ on
$O=\mathbb R\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R$ over $[0,2\pi]\times\mathbb R$
([[def-cm-time-dependent-lagrangian-and-action]]), and consider the variations

$$\eta_1(t)=\sin\frac t2,\qquad\eta_3(t)=\sin\frac{3t}{2}$$

of the zero curve $q_0\equiv0$. The proposition [[prop-cm-oscillator-second-variation-signs]]
gives

$$\delta^2S(q_0)[\eta_1,\eta_1]=-\frac{3\pi}{4}<0,\qquad\delta^2S(q_0)[\eta_3,\eta_3]=\frac{5\pi}{4}>0,$$

and with the exact identity $S(\varepsilon\eta)=\frac{\varepsilon^2}{2}\delta^2S(q_0)[\eta,\eta]$
of that proposition,

$$S(\varepsilon\eta_1)=-\frac{3\pi\varepsilon^2}{8}<0<\frac{5\pi\varepsilon^2}{8}=S(\varepsilon\eta_3)\qquad(\varepsilon\ne0).$$

Thus at the duration $T=2\pi>\pi=\pi/\omega$ the stationary zero curve has variations that
decrease and variations that increase the action arbitrarily close to it: it is a saddle, and
neither a local minimiser nor a local maximiser. Every number below is exact; no measurement or
numerical integration is involved.
items.strategy: Substitute T=2pi and omega=1 in the second-variation formula, evaluate the two trigonometric integrals independently as a check, and read the saddle behaviour off the exact action identity.

items.title: Two distinct oscillator solutions with the same zero endpoints at $T=\pi$, and their common action value
items.reference: batch-12-constructed-B-example; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement:
Take $m=1$, $k=1$, hence $\omega=1$, and $T=\pi$ in
[[prop-cm-oscillator-boundary-value-nonuniqueness]], and consider the two curves

$$x_1(t)=\sin t,\qquad x_2(t)=2\sin t\qquad(t\in[0,\pi]).$$

Both are $C^\infty$ solutions of $x''+x=0$ on $[0,\pi]$ with $x(0)=x(\pi)=0$, and they are
distinct; they have different initial velocities $1$ and $2$. On the chart
$\mathcal L(q,v)=\tfrac12(v^2-q^2)$ over $[0,\pi]\times\mathbb R$
([[def-cm-time-dependent-lagrangian-and-action]]) both are stationary curves of the action, and
their action values agree:

$$S(x_1)=S(x_2)=0.$$

This is the concrete $T=\pi$ case of the non-uniqueness in
[[prop-cm-oscillator-boundary-value-nonuniqueness]] and of the signed-action checks of
[[ex-cm-oscillator-saddle-second-variation-checks]]; all numbers are exact.
items.strategy: Verify the two solutions and their boundary data, note distinctness and the differing initial velocities, and evaluate the action along the family with the double-angle formula and the fundamental theorem of calculus.

items.title: Parallel-axis theorem checked on two equal point masses on the third axis
items.reference: batch-12-constructed-B-example; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement:
Let $m>0$, $r>0$, and let

$$\nu:=m\,\delta_{r e_3}+m\,\delta_{-r e_3}$$

be the weighted sum of the two Dirac measures at $\pm re_3$ ([[def-dirac-measure]],
[[thm-nonnegative-weighted-sums-of-measures]]), a bounded finite Borel measure and hence a mass
distribution of total mass $2m$ ([[def-cm-mass-distribution-and-inertia-matrix]]). Assume the
Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), used only to make the
displayed integrals finite ([[lem-cm-inertia-tensor-about-a-point-is-finite]],
[[lem-cm-mass-moments-are-finite]]). Then:

- $\nu$ is centred, $\mu(\nu)=m\,re_3+m(-re_3)=0$, and its inertia matrix about the origin is
  $I(\nu)=\mathrm{diag}(2mr^2,2mr^2,0)$;
- the inertia tensor about $a=ce_3$, computed directly from the definition, is
  $I_\nu(ce_3)=\mathrm{diag}(2m(r^2+c^2),2m(r^2+c^2),0)$, and the parallel-axis identity of
  [[thm-cm-parallel-axis-theorem]], $I_\nu(a)=I(\nu)+2m(\lVert a\rVert_2^2I_3-aa^{\mathsf T})$,
  reproduces exactly this value.

All entries are exact polynomial expressions in $m,r,c$; no measurement is involved.
items.strategy: Evaluate the atomic integrals against the two Dirac measures, compute the shifted inertia tensor directly at a=c e_3, and compare with the parallel-axis formula.

items.title: Two-mass spring eigenmodes at explicit parameters: eigenrelations, a mode solution, and the zero-frequency case
items.reference: batch-12-constructed-B-example; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement:
Take $m=1$, $k=1$, $c=3$ in [[prop-cm-two-mass-spring-modes]], so that
$K=\begin{pmatrix}4&-3\\-3&4\end{pmatrix}$ and
$u_\pm=\frac1{\sqrt2}(1,\pm1)^{\mathsf T}$; the proposition gives $Ku_+=u_+$ and $Ku_-=7u_-$, hence
squared frequencies $k/m=1$ and $(k+2c)/m=7$. The curve

$$x(t)=\cos(t)\,u_++\cos(\sqrt7\,t)\,u_-$$

solves $x''=-Kx$ with $x(0)=(\sqrt2,0)$ and $x'(0)=0$. In the degenerate case $k=0$, $c=1$ one has
$K=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $Ku_+=0$, so $x(t)=(1+t)u_+$ solves $x''=-Kx$ and
is unbounded on $[0,\infty)$: the zero-frequency mode is affine, not oscillatory. All entries are
exact; no numerical integration or measurement is involved.
items.strategy: Multiply the two explicit matrices into the eigenvectors, substitute the eigenrelations into the mode solution and differentiate, and check the degenerate affine mode.

items.title: The pendulum linearisation bound at $g=l=1$: exact error bound for the data $\delta=1/100$, $T=1$
items.reference: batch-12-constructed-B-example; recorded in the batch notes
items.statement:
Take $g=l=1$ in [[prop-cm-pendulum-small-angle-linearization-bound]], so that $\omega=1$,
$F(\theta,v)=(v,-\sin\theta)$, $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $L=1$ and
$\lVert A\rVert=1$. Choose the ball radius $r=1/2$, the datum
$z_0=(\delta,0)$ with $\delta=1/100$, and the horizon $T=1$. Then
$\delta e^{LT}=e/100<3/100<1/2=r$ because $2<e<3$
([[cor-two-less-than-e-less-than-three]]), so the proposition applies and gives

$$\lVert z(t)-y(t)\rVert_2\le\frac{1}{12\cdot10^4}\bigl(e^{2t}-e^{t}\bigr)\qquad(0\le t\le1),$$

where $y(t)=\delta(\cos t,-\sin t)$ solves $y'=Ay$, $y(0)=z_0$; at $t=1$ the bound reads
$(e^2-e)/(12\cdot10^4)$ and is at most $e^3/(12\cdot10^4)$. The remainder checks at
$\lVert z\rVert_2\le r$ are: $\lvert\sin\theta-\theta\rvert\le\lvert\theta\rvert^3/6\le1/48$, and
$\lvert\sin\theta\rvert\le\lvert\theta\rvert\le r=1/2$. All constants are exact; the single
inequality $e<3$ is the only numerical input.
items.strategy: Instantiate the proposition at the stated constants, verify the smallness condition with the published bound on e, evaluate the integral by the fundamental theorem, and check the pointwise remainder bounds.
